title: Jets and explosions in NGC 7793
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 7793, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA Acknowledgement: D. Calzetti (University of Massachusetts) and the LEGUS Team

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows the spiral arms and small central bulge of NGC 7793, crossed by a mottled pattern of dark dust. Its spiral structure is not strongly defined, and occasional bursts of bright pink mark stellar nurseries where new stars are forming. It lies in the constellation Sculptor, some 13 million light-years away according to the caption.

The calm appearance hides a violent object. Astronomers have found a powerful microquasar in the galaxy, a black hole feeding on material from a companion star. Full-sized quasars sit at galaxy centres, so finding one in a galaxy's disc is unusual.

Microquasars are like scale models that let astronomers study quasars up close. Material falling toward the black hole forms a swirling disc, and some of it is flung outward at very high speed in two opposite jets. In NGC 7793 the jets are blowing an expanding bubble of hot gas some 1,000 light-years across.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the microquasar itself is not something the image shows directly.

explore: NGC 7793 ranks among the brightest members of the Sculptor Group, one of the nearest galaxy groups to our Local Group, which contains the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds.
alt: A spiral galaxy with a weakly defined spiral pattern, a small bulge, mottled dark dust and scattered pink patches.
